title: Made in Canada: Negotiation, Trust and the Room You're Not In, with Fotini Iconomopoulos

host.name: Nola Simon
host.title: Futurist & Founder, Everyday Futurism
host.credentials: 17 years in cross-border insurance operations · Creator of the Assumption-Ground Audit

guest.name: Fotini Iconomopoulos
guest.title: Negotiation expert
guest.credentials: Author of Say Less, Get More · Adjunct professor of MBA Negotiations at the Schulich School of Business · Works with women executives through Next Up (formerly the Network of Executive Women)

abstract: Fotini Iconomopoulos, negotiation expert and author of Say Less, Get More, explains why your raise is decided months before you hear about it, and why the people who are not in the room have to work harder to send the trust signals that being in the room used to send for them. The conversation covers working backwards from what you want, building warmth through a screen, the line between monitoring for liability and monitoring that signals distrust, why most women she works with are collaborative negotiators, how even a junior person holds power, and the value of being comfortable with silence.
takeaways: Map the timeline backwards: know what you want and when, then name the milestones, the decision makers and the blackout periods along the way.
Run the relationship-building that online meetings skip. In person, a meeting starts at the lobby, the coffee and the walk to the boardroom; on video, build that warmth back in on purpose.
Interrogate monitoring: some exists for regulatory and liability reasons, but past that point it reads as distrust and people stop doing their best work.
Surface your power, even as a junior person. The more someone depends on you, the more power you have in the negotiation.
Audit when your raise is really decided. Salary decisions are made months before December, so plant seeds, gather data and find champions who speak for you in rooms you are not in.

keyQA.question: When is your raise actually negotiated?
keyQA.answer: Months before you hear about it. Fotini Iconomopoulos explains that if you are told about a raise on December 1, executives sat in a room a month or more earlier dividing up the budget, and before that your manager either spoke up about your achievements or did not. The negotiation started back in August and September.

keyQA.question: Does working remotely hurt women's careers?
keyQA.answer: Fotini does not see it as a conscious penalty. It is how the brain works: the frequency of contact shapes our impressions, and people in the office run into leaders in the elevator and the kitchen. People working remotely need to make extra effort to keep those relationships strong, through more frequent check-ins or occasional time in the office.

keyQA.question: Why do companies that monitor remote staff lose them?
keyQA.answer: Close monitoring is a very clear signal of distrust. Some monitoring exists for regulatory reasons, which is a liability issue rather than a trust issue, but when people feel they are held under a microscope, they do not do their best work and the company is likely to lose them.

keyQA.question: What does Say Less, Get More mean?
keyQA.answer: Stop talking and let other people give you valuable information. Pause long enough for rational thought to come back before you talk yourself out of a deal, and use the pause to be more self-aware of what is happening with you and others in the room.
